EFT is a batch electronic bank transfer cleared through Payments Canada, usually 1 to 3 business days, low cost, and it can be returned if something is wrong. A wire is a single payment sent same day for large or urgent amounts, with higher fees, and it is effectively final once sent. Merchant payouts are normally EFT, so a deck that says 'wire' for a standard payout is wrong.
Action: Draft a two-line definition you can paste into the sales deck or send to the team.

I'll look for a plumber near Leslieville with good reviews who can do a dripping outside tap and a hose bib that won't shut off, today or Monday. In the meantime, if there's an inside shut-off for that line, closing it will stop the drip.
Action: Search for plumbers near Leslieville with decent reviews and availability today or Monday, and send you the top three with prices and next openings so you can pick one to book.

Here's a tighter version: 'If a payout fails because of a bank-side error, the system automatically retries it, with no action needed from the merchant.' It keeps the same requirement in one sentence and drops the passive 'caused by' and 'being required'.

ACH is the US term; Canada's equivalent is EFT, batch bank-to-bank transfers cleared through Payments Canada, covering things like direct deposit and pre-authorized debits. On a Canadian call people usually use them to mean the same thing, though strictly ACH is the US network and EFT is the Canadian one.
Action: Save a two-line version in your notes so the distinction is handy next time it comes up.

Dry sweeping really can make drywall dust worse, since it grinds the fine dust into the finish and puts it back in the air, so Sam isn't alone in that. Use a vacuum with a soft hardwood brush head and the beater bar off, then go over it with a barely damp microfiber mop and dry the floor right away. And I'm here for the talk too, however long this kitchen stretch has felt.

She should compare what she'd net from selling (price minus realtor and legal costs, any mortgage penalty, and possible capital gains tax) against what renting would net after condo fees, property tax, insurance, vacancy and tax on the rent. Then the softer questions: does she want to be a landlord, could the sale money earn more elsewhere, would she want to move back in, and does the condo or her mortgage restrict renting. A rough one-year side-by-side usually makes the decision clearer.
Action: Put this into a short checklist you can send to Jess.
